content:
Code reportedly found in the latest iOS 27 beta's camera app suggests several major professional photography and videography features are coming soon.

Although the built-in camera app has steadily gained features, the discovery seems surprising for an app designed primarily for point-and-shoot photography...

Apple has always tried to strike a balance—on one hand, making its own camera app extremely easy to use for casual snapshots, while on the other giving users who like to take photography seriously a degree of creative control. However, despite the gradual evolution of this app, most serious photographers and videographers still prefer to use third-party apps.

If these findings prove accurate, some powerful features usually associated with professional cameras are about to be added, which could change the situation. Developer pdfu says they found code supporting four main features, none of which have been enabled in any beta version.

Exposure Monitoring Tools

Judging exposure by eye alone is prone to error, especially when viewing the iPhone screen in harsh sunlight. Most professional cameras support a histogram function that accurately reflects exposure status, while video editing software typically uses waveforms to display the same type of information. Pdfu says they found code for both features in the beta.

Focus Peaking

The depth of field range from near to far in a photo is affected by many factors, but in some scenes only part of the range is in focus. Similarly, judging by eye alone where focus is sharp and where it is not is very unreliable, so professional cameras in particular often use a method called focus peaking.

With this feature enabled, you can turn on an overlay marking that highlights the in-focus parts of the image, usually in red—although the example on the left uses yellow.

Highlight Overexposure Warning

The biggest risk of exposure errors is overexposure. Generally speaking, if shadows are underexposed, they can usually be rescued in post-processing—unless so severely that the dark areas turn completely black (RGB value of zero). Overexposure is much more troublesome, because highlights easily blow out completely, meaning bright areas exceed RGB 255 and cannot be recovered in post.

Many professional cameras use an indicator called zebra stripes, which uses red diagonal lines to mark fully blown-out areas. Some cameras let you manually set this threshold so you receive a warning when you are approaching overexposure (for example, reaching 90%), rather than only being alerted once you have actually blown out.

This feature is also shown on the right in the image above.

Manual Focus

Although the current camera app lets you lock focus on a subject in the frame, it can only lock exposure and focus together at the same point via AE/AF lock (auto exposure/auto focus).

Reports say Apple has tested using a slider to achieve true manual focus in the camera app. Pdfu says this feature may be limited to one or more upcoming new iPhones.

Other Features

In addition to the professional features, an option is reportedly being added to take a burst of countdown selfies. When taking group photos, many people always want to take a few more shots; this feature lets you place your iPhone on a tripod or fix it in a certain position, then take multiple photos in succession and pick the one everyone is happy with.

Finally, there are indications a new image processing method will be adopted to go with the variable aperture expected on the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac's Take

The features mentioned above are not enabled in any iOS 27 beta, and I am surprised Apple would put them in the built-in camera app rather than restricting them to Final Cut Camera, but the report looks credible.

What do you think of this report? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
